approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would add a new purpose to aviation and maritime security laws to stop serious crime at airports, ports, and offshore oil and gas facilities.
It would let the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission conduct criminal intelligence checks for security identification card schemes, with reviews in the Administrative Appeals Tribunal.
Regulations made under the new purpose could set fines of up to 200 penalty units, matching existing penalty levels in the card schemes.
Creates an extra purpose in the Aviation Transport Security Act 2004 and the Maritime Transport and Offshore Facilities Security Act 2003 to prevent serious crime.
Allows regulations for that purpose to prescribe penalties of up to 200 penalty units.
Clarifies the legal basis for background checks under the aviation and maritime Acts.
Gives the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission the function of doing criminal intelligence assessments for the card schemes.
Adds criminal intelligence assessments as a fifth element of background checks under the AusCheck Act 2007.
Exempts decisions on those assessments from judicial review under the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977.
People who apply for or renew aviation or maritime security identification cards, and the agencies that run the card schemes.

The Transport Security Amendment (Serious Crime) Bill 2019 will make people convicted of serious offences ineligible for Aviation Security Identification Cards (ASIC) and Maritime Security Identification Cards (MSIC), targeting nearly 300 current cardholders with known criminal links and aiming to prevent organised crime from exploiting airports and seaports.

The Labor opposition argued the bill is unfit for purpose, citing the lack of a definition for "serious crime" and stricter rules for Australian workers than foreign crews. They announced amendments to define serious crime, mandate processing times for security cards, provide avenues of appeal, and require similar background checks for foreign crew, while also criticising the government’s border failures over the Ruby Princess and stranded Australians.

The Transport Security Amendment (Serious Crime) Bill 2019 will amend aviation and maritime security acts to exclude people with serious criminal convictions or links to organised crime from holding ASIC and MSIC cards, addressing a gap where background checks only considered security threats. The speaker noted that 227 existing cardholders were on the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission's National Criminal Target List and cited cases where the Administrative Appeals Tribunal granted cards to convicted criminals.

The speaker argued that activities like posting a Facebook protest, going to the beach, or holding a sign should never be considered serious crimes, while citing child sexual abuse (with a 100% increase during lockdowns reported by the AFP) and denial of medical treatment as actual serious crimes. They supported the Transport Security Amendment (Serious Crime) Bill 2019, noting organised crime costs Australia $47 billion annually, and urged its passage with a Senate committee amendment.

The government argued the Transport Security Amendment (Serious Crime) Bill 2019 would strengthen aviation and maritime security by allowing refusal of ASIC and MSIC applications to those with serious criminal histories. The speaker announced amendments to include criminal intelligence assessments, citing 845 drug-induced deaths in 2018 and $47 billion annual cost of organised crime.

Operation Ironside led to 268 charges, 627 offences, nearly four tonnes of drugs seized and over $51 million in cash confiscated. The government called for passage of the Transport Security Amendment (Serious Crime) Bill to tighten security checks at airports and wharves, noting over 220 workers in secure areas are on national criminal or gangs lists.

The government announced the passage of the Transport Security Amendment (Serious Crime) Bill through the Senate, requiring stricter background checks for workers in secure areas of airports and wharves to prevent organised crime links, while reaffirming its commitment to strong border security.
